catalog_quote: Generally speaking, Saafi words are stressed on the penultimate syllable. While stress in Saafi is an area that merits much further investigation, there are two important principles of stress systems that seem to play a role in Saafi prosody. This first principle is defined in (22). (22) STRESS-TO-WEIGHT: stressed syllables are heavy. Generally speaking, Saafi words are stressed on the penultimate syllable. Therefore, when a monomoraic syllable is in penultimate position, the vowel will lengthen. When a bimoraic syllable is in penultimate position, however, no lengthening will occur. ... (23) [ˈjɑːndɛr] ‘door’ [jɑnˈdɛːri] ‘the door’ [ˈɗoːpat] ‘animal’ [ɗo.ˈpat.ci] ‘the animal’ ... This pattern, however, seems to be outranked by the principle presented in (24): (24) WEIGHT-TO-STRESS: heavy syllables are stressed. When heavy syllables are in word-final position, they tend to attract the stress away from the penultimate syllable. ... (25) [inɑ.ˈtɑŋ] ‘wild animal’ [mbɑm.ˈħuħ] ‘pig’ [muː.mɑ.ˈniː] ‘this lion’ [muː.mɑ.ˈcɛm] ‘those lions’ A broad generalization of the Saafi stress system is that stressed syllables are either in penultimate or final position, and that the langauge chooses between these two positions based on syllable weight. This is not without exceptions, however (voiceless heavily aspirated word-initial consonants tend to attract stress), and any further analysis of the stress system is beyond the scope of this section.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penultimate syllable; a heavy (closed or long-vowelled) word-final syllable attracts stress to the final syllable (e.g. ina.'tang 'wild animal', mbam.'huh 'pig', muu.ma.'nii 'this lion'); a stressed light penult lengthens its vowel ('jaan.der 'door' vs jan.'dee.ri 'the door'). Independently, Piquero 2011 (same consultant, same field-methods class) p. 8-9 states plain penultimate stress for 2-5 syllable words without mentioning the final-heavy attraction.
new_statements.exceptions: Stanton: 'voiceless heavily aspirated word-initial consonants tend to attract stress'; deictic (demonstrative) suffixes always take primary stress (p. 46, sec. 2.3.1); vowel-length vs stress-lengthening interaction left unresolved (sec. 1.5.2). Piquero: none.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from elicitation with one consultant. Stanton sec. 1.5.3 additionally reports phrase-conditioned stress: in multi-word NPs ('the two hot fires', 'the new black book') each word carries initial stress, overriding the penultimate/final preference. Language explicitly described as non-tonal (Stanton p. 7).
new_statements.identity_note: Both open sketches (Stanton 2011, Piquero 2011) come from one Indiana University field-methods class with a single consultant, Adrien Pouille (from Tchis near Thiès; the Botne & Pouille dictionary labels his speech the 'Sébikotane variety'). Stanton lists five dialects (Boukhou, Sebikotane, Sindia, Hasab, Diobass); Mbodj 1983 describes Boukhou. No separate Glottolog dialect codes seen; all under saaf1238. Stanton also lists Pouille as a childhood L2 learner of Saafi (L1 Wolof/French), which lowers confidence.
